anti_generic_signature_read: Asked what stops this being an off-the-shelf version of whatever it decided it was: 'The most distinctive thing is the sculpted terrain: crater dishes actually scooped into the tiles with pips around their rims, and free-standing cones rising off the sand and ice squares. That is the one element that makes this not a re-skinned chess set. The second-best thing is the tray-of-scoops, which turns storage into part of the object.' It marked the two sunburst areas as a repeated motif and a genericness weakness, then withdrew that itself on learning they are the two stars: 'Same structure in two colours is now correct rather than lazy.'
blind_action_read: 'Nothing is hinged, geared or sprung. The action is lift-and-place: sixteen pieces on plinths that invite being picked up by the ball and moved between recessed squares, and two trays whose eight scoops each are obviously sized to receive those balls at pack-away.' That is the correct read: nothing in this set moves against anything else, and no motion is claimed.
blind_form_read: 'The playing squares are sunken -- each tile sits in a recess and you can see the shadow line around every one ... the orange-brown tiles have dished circular craters scooped INTO them with small pointed pips standing proud around the edges ... I read all of that as real relief rather than paint because each dish and each cone casts its own shadow and breaks the tile silhouette. The plinths are short solid cylinders ... The spheres are true balls, each on a short cylindrical neck/collar that plugs into the plinth.' It first read Neptune's white bands as raised ribs and its dark spot as flat paint, then withdrew that in full when the solids were measured: 'Both are flush inlays at +0.000000 mm. I withdraw that entirely.'
blind_held_read: Unprompted, before anything was revealed: 'This is a board game. A thick grey square-tiled board with sculpted terrain, sixteen ball-shaped playing pieces each standing on its own round plinth, split into a white-plinth army and a black-plinth army, plus two matching storage trays with scooped hollows to park the pieces in. Handed the physical thing I would say: a two-player abstract strategy game -- chess-like in layout, solar-system themed -- where each side commands eight planets across a terrain grid.' It also counted the sides itself: 'the pedestals come in precisely two finishes' and 'eight pieces per side, eight scoops per tray, two trays.'
blind_relationship_read: 'Board carries plinths; plinths carry balls; trays receive balls. The grid carries recessed terrain tiles which the plinths stand on or beside. The two groups are distinguished solely by plinth colour -- white versus black -- with identical spheres between them. That is a clean and legible scheme, and the counts match: eight pieces per side, eight scoops per tray, two trays.' It also read the lean unaided -- 'presumably modelling axial tilt' -- from the polar frame showing the camera looking straight down the ball's own axis.
blind_subjects_read: Named unprompted, with the cue each came from: 'Saturn (pale yellow ball with a flat encircling disc -- unmistakable), Jupiter (orange ball, horizontal bands, one red oval spot), Earth (small blue ball with green landmasses and white polar patches), Mars (small red ball with a white cap), and a gas or ice giant, blue with pale bands and a dark oval which I would have called Neptune unaided.' It was equally plain about what did not arrive: Uranus 'does not self-identify -- unaided I would have described it as a cyan ball with a seam and a large grey sticker', and Mercury and Venus it could not name at all.

critical_form_requirements.blind_evidence: Blind, before anything was revealed, the critic counted the pale marks on the blue ball and re-traced them under challenge: 'I now count three, and I have to correct my round-1 hedge of three or four ... band 1 is the tight outer arc over the upper left; band 2 sweeps from ~(310,145) down and right to the limb at ~(700,380); band 3 crosses low from ~(350,470) to ~(695,455). Three.' Three again in four other frames, and 'neptune-sol-polar.png shows two closed concentric circles -- the near-pole band and the equatorial band at the limb, with the third below the horizon. That is exactly the signature of three bands, not four.'
critical_form_requirements.requirement: Neptune's white cloud marking is THREE closed latitude bands at -46/-41, +11/+15 and +30/+33, in `white`, as one marking with one key -- the three the build carried before the cloud correction, restored verbatim.

critical_form_requirements.blind_evidence: Blind: 'Do they go all the way round? Yes, certainly. Two independent proofs are in the set. The polar views show them as closed, complete circles with no break anywhere around. And the opposite views show bands on the far hemisphere too -- neptune-sol-opposite.png carries three bands across a face that has no spot on it, so the bands are not confined to one front.'
critical_form_requirements.requirement: Each band is CLOSED: it runs the whole way round the planet rather than starting and stopping.

critical_form_requirements.blind_evidence: Blind: 'One flat grey ellipse -- a single dark oval, present on one hemisphere only and completely absent from the opposite side.' It tracked the spot across six frames and confirmed it 'moves position between images exactly as a single fixed spot on a re-oriented ball should'. Measured on the 4x crop: '245 px wide by 129 px tall, 1.9:1', and 'in the lower hemisphere in all six views where it appears'.
critical_form_requirements.requirement: The Great Dark Spot does not move: one clean `dark_gray` oval about twice as wide as it is tall, south of the equator, unchanged from the build this revision corrects.

critical_form_requirements.blind_evidence: Blind, and then traced deliberately: 'I traced every pale mark in all eight Neptune-bearing frames. Each one either reaches the silhouette at both ends, or is cut by the collar.' It named its own one candidate and disposed of it: in neptune-sol-spot.png 'band C appears to stop around (370,595). It does not -- the collar's top edge is at y~595 there, and the band re-emerges at the right limb around (660,455)-(710,490). That is occlusion, not a break.'
critical_form_requirements.requirement: NO short cloud streaks, wisps or arcs anywhere on Neptune: no white mark that starts and stops partway round the ball.

critical_form_requirements.blind_evidence: Blind, unprompted, listing what is on the surface: 'Besides the bands and that one spot, nothing.' On re-examination at 4x magnification: 'the blue immediately around the ellipse is clean in all directions, no second pale mark within the crop's field. Same in neptune-anti-spot.png around (550,455).' Shown the reference photograph afterwards, it noted the omission is deliberate: 'the reference does carry a pale streak just below-right of its spot; the piece correctly omits it.'
critical_form_requirements.requirement: NO bright companion cloud beside the dark spot.

critical_form_requirements.blind_evidence: Blind: 'a single dark oval, present on one hemisphere only and completely absent from the opposite side (neptune-sol-opposite.png and neptune-anti-opposite.png are bare of it)'. Confirmed again on the comparison round: 'the opposite hemisphere completely bare of any dark mark. One spot only.'
critical_form_requirements.requirement: NO second dark spot anywhere on Neptune.

critical_form_requirements.blind_evidence: Blind: 'No moons, no rings, no text, no polar cap.' Checked frame by frame afterwards: 'neptune-sol-polar.png and neptune-anti-polar.png look straight down the axis. Inside the innermost band the surface is plain blue with the ordinary shading gradient and nothing brighter at the centre'; 'nothing breaks the Neptune silhouette in any of the eight frames, and no encircling line sits off the surface'; and on the spot's interior, 'flat uniform grey, edge to edge, zero internal structure.'
critical_form_requirements.requirement: NO polar brightening, NO ring or ring arc, and NO darker centre inside the dark spot, on Neptune.

critical_form_requirements.blind_evidence: The critic reported the opposite of softening, unprompted, and read it as the harder choice: 'The bands are hard-edged (one-pixel white-to-blue step in the 4x crop), constant-width, high-contrast, and closed. Nothing is feathered, tapered, thinned at the limbs, or interrupted. If anything, this edition took the harder road: the hard edge and full width are precisely what produces the beach-ball read, and they were not touched. I can see no sign of a compromise having been made.'
critical_form_requirements.requirement: The bands were NOT softened, moved, narrowed or broken to make the blind reading come out nicer.

critical_form_requirements.blind_evidence: Blind, from the side-by-side frame: 'Same diameter, same three bands, same single grey oval, and the lean is opposite: the white-plinth ball's pole comes toward the viewer's upper left with the bands wrapping tight around it, the black-plinth ball's bands run as three open diagonals rising left-to-right.' It stated its own limit honestly -- it can confirm opposite lean and identical markings from renders but not distinguish a mirror from a rotation, which `measure/neptune-mirror.md` settles on the solids instead.
critical_form_requirements.requirement: The two Neptune pieces are mirrors of each other: same ball, same markings, obliquity mirrored.

critical_form_requirements.blind_evidence: Answered blind, before the requirement was known: 'clearly two different pieces, at arm's length, in ordinary light ... Colour, first and decisively. Left is a saturated mid-blue; right is a bright pale turquoise. That gap is wide enough to read across a room ... Surface, second. Left has multiple thin diagonal stripes plus a small dark oval; right has one big pale blob and a single seam-like rib.' It was equally plain that size does not help: 'They are the same diameter to my eye.'
critical_form_requirements.requirement: Neptune stays distinguishable from Uranus at board distance, on silhouette and on surface.

critical_form_requirements.blind_evidence: Answered blind: 'not even close -- instantly two different things. Earth is roughly two-thirds the diameter of the blue ball, and it is multicoloured with irregular green shapes on blue. Size does the work first here, and pattern confirms it. This pair separates far more strongly than the Uranus pair does.' It also separated all three worlds on sight at board scale in `iso.png` with no priming.
critical_form_requirements.requirement: Neptune stays distinguishable from Earth at board distance, on silhouette and on surface.

critical_form_requirements.blind_evidence: Checked piece by piece against its own blind description: 'Uranus: upright ring present in neptune-uranus-hero.png and -anti.png, and in both iso.png copies. Pale polar region present at ~(720,300) ... Saturn: flat encircling disc present on both copies ... Jupiter (bands + red oval), Earth (green landmasses), Mars (red + white cap), and the two small pieces I could not name blind are all present in both armies, eight a side, appearance identical to my blind description. The board, the crater tiles with their scooped dishes and rim pips, both stars, and both eight-scoop trays are all as I described them.'
critical_form_requirements.requirement: Nothing else in the set changed: Uranus keeps its upright ring and its polar hoods, Saturn keeps its flat ring, and the other worlds, the four board panels, the belt tiles, the corona cells, the two stars and the two trays are as they were.

largest_risk: The critic's, in its own words and not softened. Asked cold, before anything was revealed, whether any piece in the whole-set render reads as a beach ball or a tennis ball, it named Neptune and only Neptune: 'Yes, one piece, in both its copies. The medium-blue ball with thin pale stripes ... Both read to me as a beach ball rather than a tennis ball.' In the per-world hero frame it went further -- 'there I'd call it a tennis ball, because two narrow curved seams sweeping around a coloured ball IS the tennis-ball signature.' Told afterwards that the owner was warned of exactly this and chose it anyway, it did not move: 'Yes. Unchanged. Knowing it was predicted and accepted does not make the ball look different.' WHAT IT DIAGNOSED, which is the sentence the owner acts on: the read is NOT caused by the tilt and NOT by there being three bands -- the reference photograph has markings at the same latitudes and the same lean and does not read as a beach ball. It is caused by three surface properties the reference does not share: a one-pixel hard edge where the reference's clouds are feathered; a constant width of about 4 per cent of the ball's diameter where the reference's vary and some are hairline; and near-white on saturated blue where the reference is 15-20 per cent brighter than its own globe. The tilt is the ownership cue and cannot be given up. If anyone wants to move this reading without giving up closed bands, contrast is where the room is.
resolution: Four review rounds, ZERO repairs, one independent critic, and NO geometry changed at any point: the images reviewed in round 1 are the images sealed here. Round 1 was unprimed and identified the object, the two armies, the lift-and-place action and the axial tilt, and answered this revision's own decisive question -- does any piece read as a beach ball -- with yes, naming Neptune. That answer is the owner's expected outcome, is recorded in `largest_risk` rather than repaired, and the bands were not touched. Rounds 2-4 were disclosed comparison rounds. SIX OF THE CRITIC'S TWELVE BLIND FINDINGS WERE OVERTURNED BY MEASUREMENT AND WITHDRAWN IN WRITING, not argued away: the white bands and the dark spot are both flush inlays at +0.000000 mm proud of a 10.945000 mm globe radius, not ribs versus paint ('I withdraw that entirely'); the dark spot is a whole unbroken ellipse at the hero frame, not half-swallowed by the collar; `iso.png` has an even 48-pixel margin and nothing is clipped; the proud tan slab and the black tile are the two stars, deliberate and symmetric; the plinth numeral is upright, not rotated. Two more were reclassified as renderer artefacts. Its own closing note: 'wherever the design's correctness depended on a fact I didn't have ... I read the deliberate decision as an error.' Four findings stand as non-blocking observations on parts this revision did not touch. No blocking defect against any requirement. Print status is sealed `digitally-verified-not-print-ready` with `print_ready_claim: false` and an empty print-gate map; motion is unverified, never passed.
reviewer: One independent native critic, four rounds, shown only the fifteen canonical renders. Round 1 was fully unprimed; rounds 2-4 are disclosed re-reviews on unchanged geometry, not naive reads.
